title: The Ethics of Care
objective: After this level you can explain the ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan and Nel Noddings and why it starts from relationships rather than rules.
summary: Gilligan heard a voice of care that Kohlberg’s model missed, and Noddings built an ethics starting from caring relationships; critics call it a slave morality or parochial.

cards.headline: Should a man steal a drug he can’t afford to save his wife?
cards.body: Two 11-year-olds answered in very different ways. One psychologist heard a whole ethics in the difference.

cards.headline: A different voice
cards.body: Lawrence Kohlberg’s studies pictured moral growth as a climb toward universal principles, and girls tended to score lower. Carol Gilligan, whose mentor he was, blamed the map, not the girls. In In a Different Voice (1982), she argued that his model was biased, and that it had mistaken a voice of care for immaturity.

cards.headline: Jake and Amy
cards.body: The case was Kohlberg’s Heinz dilemma. Jake, 11, treated it as a math problem with people: life outranks property, so Heinz should steal. Amy, 11, said no. If Heinz went to jail, his wife could end up worse off. She saw relationships stretching over time, and wanted Heinz and the druggist to talk it out and find the money another way.

cards.headline: Starting from relationships
cards.body: The philosopher Nel Noddings built the view out in Caring (1984). Ethics starts from a relationship between the one-caring and the cared-for. Caring means engrossment: taking in the other person on their own terms. Noddings rejected universal principles for prescribed action; care must fit the case. That sets care ethics apart from Kantian and utilitarian ethics alike.

cards.headline: Critics of care
cards.body: Critics raised sharp worries. Some call care ethics a slave morality, borrowing Nietzsche’s term: it praises self-giving traits shaped by women’s oppression. Others call it parochial, favoring those nearby over distant strangers. Noddings herself later endorsed a stronger obligation to care about distant people.

cards.headline: The Ethics of Care: the big picture
learned: Gilligan: Kohlberg’s map missed a voice of care
Jake saw math; Amy saw relationships
Noddings: the one-caring and the cared-for
Critics: slave morality, or too parochial

questions.prompt: In Noddings’s ethics of care, who are the two parties in a caring relationship?
questions.explanation: Noddings describes caring as a relationship between the one-caring and the cared-for.

questions.prompt: Why did Amy say Heinz shouldn’t steal the drug?

options.label: Jail could leave his wife worse off, so they should talk it out
The druggist deserved his profit
options.rationale: She didn’t argue from the druggist’s rights.

options.label: Stealing always breaks a universal law that binds everyone
options.rationale: That’s a Kantian way of putting it, not Amy’s.

questions.explanation: Amy saw the relationships over time: jail would leave the wife worse off, so Heinz and the druggist should find another way.

questions.prompt: Noddings rejected universal principles for prescribed action. Which Level 47 test is built on exactly such a principle?

options.label: Aristotle’s golden mean
options.rationale: That’s from Level 45, and it’s relative to the person.

questions.explanation: Kant’s first test asks whether you could will your maxim as a universal law, the kind of principle Noddings rejected.
